stories.body: SAULT STE. MARIE – Monday and Tuesday were good days for limestone cargoes in the Sault Ste. Marie area. Baie Comeau and Saginaw unloaded stone for Algoma Steel’s electric arc furnaces on Tuesday, while Manitowoc unloaded stone at the Northwest Pier of the Soo Locks Tuesday morning for use in the New Soo Lock Project. After unloading, the Saginaw headed downbound for Goderich, Baie Comeau set course for Thessalon and Manitowoc was downbound late morning Tuesday and will anchor above DeTour awaiting Algoma Compass’ departure from the Drummond Island stone dock. shippingNews.postTitle: Maritime Ports are a Growing Sector of Michigan’s Economy

stories.body: LANSING, MI – Standing on the shoreline and looking out, there is only vast blue reaching to the horizon. On that horizon, a cargo ship approaches in the distance, but this is no ocean – it’s one of the Great Lakes. Michigan is surrounded by the blue depths of lakes Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie with shorelines stretching thousands of miles. Along these waters, maritime ports contribute greatly to the economic and transportation prosperity of the state. todayInHistory.title: Life Aboard the Edmund Fitzgerald Described in Letters from Cadet
todayInHistory.text: David "Cowboy" Weiss in 1974. [GLSHS] DETROIT, MI – It wasn't just the hat that earned Edmund Fitzgerald crew member David Weiss his nickname "Cowboy." It was his friend and Great Lakes Maritime Academy classmate David James, who had just watched Frank Zappa's 1971 movie "200 Motels" featuring the character Lonesome Cowboy Burt. When James saw Weiss standing outside a classroom dressed in black and wearing a cowboy hat, the nickname came easily."He looked a little different," James said. Weiss was less "bummy" than the rest of their classmates, who dressed to emulate the sailors they were training to join. The day they met, James gave Weiss his nickname "Cowboy Burt." DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit is selling letters written by a man killed in the Edmund Fitzgerald sinking in Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. The letters were written by David Weiss while he was on the Fitzgerald. The friendship between Weiss and James is chronicled in a series of letters they exchanged while out on the inland seas in 1975, when Weiss was on the Edmund Fitzgerald and James on the Walter A. Sterling. The last was sent Oct. 30, about two weeks before Weiss went down with the Edmund Fitzgerald during a storm in Lake Superior. Twenty-eight crewmates perished along with him. todayInHistory.title: Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest to Speak In Ludington
todayInHistory.text: LUDINGTON, MI – Maritime historian, author and shipwreck explorer Valerie van Heest, whose work has helped shape the visitor experience at all three Mason County Historical Society museums, will be the featured speaker at the society’s annual dinner meeting Thursday, Dec. 3. Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest. [Mason County Historical Society] Van Heest, one of Michigan’s leading maritime historians and shipwreck researchers, will present “History of the Great Lakes,” based on her new book, “A History of the Great Lakes in Twelve Shipwrecks.” The program will explore 250 years of Great Lakes history through a dozen shipwrecks, showing how these underwater discoveries reveal broader stories of conflict, settlement, innovation and change. The annual meeting will take place at the United Methodist Church of Ludington, 5810 Bryant Road. Doors will open at 5:45 p.m., with dinner beginning at 6 p.m. The society’s annual business meeting and organizational updates will follow dinner, and van Heest’s presentation will begin at 7:30 p.m. Van Heest is co-founder and president of the Michigan Shipwreck Research Association and has helped discover about 20 shipwrecks off Michigan’s west coast while participating in archaeological investigations at more than 50 shipwreck sites throughout the Great Lakes. marineWeather.synopsis: High pressure around 30.6 inches will linger over the Mid-Atlantic states into Thursday, while low pressure around 29.5 inches moves from the northern Rockies into northwestern Ontario. Between these systems, south southwest winds are expected over Lake Michigan. A few south southwesterly gales are possible over the north half of the lake Wednesday afternoon through Thursday. Trends will be monitored, and a gale headline may be become necessary. Another low pressure system around 29.5 inches will move from the northern Plains into areas north of Lake Superior Friday into Saturday. Strong southerly winds are expected ahead of the cold front Friday night into Saturday night, with some gales possible. Gusty west to northwest winds are expected to arrive behind the front Sunday into Monday, with some gales possible Sunday.
High pressure, 30.50 inches, over Ohio will drift southeast through Thursday. Subsequently, dry weather with light to moderate southwest winds will prevail through the rest of the workweek.
High pressure 30.50 inches will persist over the Ohio Valley and Great Lakes this week before a cold front moves through the region late Sunday or early Monday.

A ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through Sunday as the embedded high pressure center persists over the Mid- Atlantic states through Friday and then moves northeastward toward New England and then Atlantic waters near Nova Scotia Friday night through this Sunday. On Sunday, a cold front should approach the lake from the Upper Midwest and eventually the central Great Lakes.
